lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can measles really erase my immune memory?
Yes. Measles doesn't just give you a rash and a fever. It slips into the cells that remember your old infections and wipes many of them out, so germs you already beat can come back.
And the timing matters. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status, held since 2000.
lines.say: And the timing matters. On November seventeenth, twenty twenty-six, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status, held since two thousand.

lines.text: That happens when one chain of measles keeps spreading for a full year. By mid-November, the CDC had counted 5,412 cases in 2026, and states had reported 10 deaths.
lines.say: That happens when one chain of measles keeps spreading for a full year. By mid-November, the C D C had counted five thousand, four hundred and twelve cases in twenty twenty-six, and states had reported ten deaths.

lines.text: Canada lost the same status a year earlier, in November 2025. Measles is settling back into North America, one unvaccinated classroom at a time.
lines.say: Canada lost the same status a year earlier, in November twenty twenty-five. Measles is settling back into North America, one unvaccinated classroom at a time.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So what does measles actually do?
Let's start with the illness itself, then follow the virus into your immune system's memory bank.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: What happens when you catch measles?
First comes a high fever, a cough, a runny nose and red, watery eyes. It looks like a bad cold.
Two or three days later, tiny white spots appear inside the cheeks, like grains of salt on red skin. Doctors call them Koplik spots, and they're a giveaway for measles.
Then the rash erupts. Flat red blotches start at the hairline and spread down the face, the neck, the chest, all the way to the feet.
About one in five unvaccinated Americans who catch measles ends up in the hospital.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Is it usually just a rash?
Not always. Up to one in twenty children with measles gets pneumonia, as the lungs fill with fluid. That's the most common way measles kills young children.
Overall, about one to three of every thousand children who catch it die from lung or brain complications.
In about one in a thousand cases, the virus inflames the brain. That's encephalitis, and it can leave a child deaf or with lasting brain damage.
And rarely, the virus hides in the brain for years. Seven to ten years later, it wakes up as SSPE, a slow brain disease that is always fatal.
lines.say: And rarely, the virus hides in the brain for years. Seven to ten years later, it wakes up as S S P E, a slow brain disease that is always fatal.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Why does measles spread so easily?
Because it floats. A cough sprays tiny droplets into the air, and they hang there like invisible smoke.
Measles can stay in a room's air for up to two hours after the sick person has left. You can walk in later and breathe it in.
Worse, people spread it for four days before the rash appears, while they still think it's just a cold, and for four days after.
If ten unprotected people share a room with someone who has measles, up to nine of them will catch it.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How does that compare to other viruses?
Scientists use a number called R naught: how many people one case infects in a crowd with no immunity. For measles, it's often quoted at twelve to eighteen.
For the seasonal flu, it's only about one and a quarter. That's why measles is the first disease to come back when vaccination rates slip.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How does measles reach my immune memory?
Your immune memory lives in white blood cells called memory B cells and memory T cells. Each one carries a record of a germ you've met or been vaccinated against.
Measles carries a key that fits a lock on their surface, a receptor called CD150. Memory T cells carry more of these locks than fresh, untrained ones.
lines.say: Measles carries a key that fits a lock on their surface, a receptor called C D one fifty. Memory T cells carry more of these locks than fresh, untrained ones.

lines.text: So the virus heads straight for them. It unlocks the memory cells, moves in, copies itself, and the infected cells are destroyed.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Doesn't the body just replace them?
It replaces the numbers, not the records. New white blood cells flood in to fight measles, so blood counts look normal again within weeks.
But many of those new cells only know measles. The old cells that remembered your past colds, flu and other infections are gone.
It's like a library fire. The shelves get restocked fast, but with copies of one book, while the rare volumes you collected are ash.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How do we know memory really gets erased?

Surprisingly, the best evidence came from an outbreak. In 2019, a team led by Michael Mina at Harvard tested blood from 77 unvaccinated children in the Netherlands, before and after they caught measles.
lines.say: Surprisingly, the best evidence came from an outbreak. In twenty nineteen, a team led by Michael Mina at Harvard tested blood from seventy-seven unvaccinated children in the Netherlands, before and after they caught measles.

lines.text: They used a tool called VirScan. It dips a drop of blood into thousands of tiny virus fragments and reads which ones your antibodies grab.
lines.say: They used a tool called Vir Scan. It dips a drop of blood into thousands of tiny virus fragments and reads which ones your antibodies grab.

lines.text: Two months after measles, the children had lost between eleven and seventy-three percent of their antibodies against other germs.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Seventy-three percent? Of everything?
Of their antibody variety, in the hardest-hit child. Antibodies against viruses and bacteria they had already beaten, from flu viruses to common bacteria, simply vanished from the blood.
Healthy children followed over the same months kept about ninety percent of their antibody variety. So this was not normal forgetting.
Children who had a severe case tended to lose more. And in monkeys infected on purpose, roughly half their old antibodies were still missing five months later.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Does the immune system ever reset fully?
Not quickly. The same year, a team in Britain and the Netherlands, led by Velislava Petrova, read the genes of the B cells in twenty-six unvaccinated Dutch children, before and after measles.
Memory B cells built up against old infections had disappeared from the blood. And the fresh B cells that replaced them were immature, like a newborn's.
The researchers called it a more baby-like immune system. Their defenses looked less experienced, closer to an infant's than a school kid's.
Some children show signs of a weakened immune system for up to five years, even when their white blood cell counts look perfectly normal.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Does that actually make people sicker?
In ferrets, yes. Ferrets vaccinated against flu caught a measles-like virus, their flu antibodies dropped, and when flu hit them, they got sicker.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How long does the danger last?
About two to three years. In 2015, Mina's team lined up decades of death records from the United States, England and Denmark.
lines.say: About two to three years. In twenty fifteen, Mina's team lined up decades of death records from the United States, England and Denmark.

lines.text: Every measles wave was followed, about two to three years later, by a wave of children dying from other infections, the ones measles had left them open to.
When the vaccine wiped out measles, those other deaths dropped too. A puzzle that had sat there since the nineteen sixties suddenly made sense.
Mina put it simply: if your child gets measles and then pneumonia two years later, you wouldn't tie the two together. But they can be linked.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: How many deaths are we talking about?
Before vaccines, their model suggests measles may have been behind up to half of all childhood deaths from infectious disease in rich countries, mostly through this hidden shadow.
Before 1963, the U.S. saw an estimated three to four million measles cases a year, and about four to five hundred deaths from measles itself.
lines.say: Before nineteen sixty-three, the U S saw an estimated three to four million measles cases a year, and about four to five hundred deaths from measles itself.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can the vaccine cause the same amnesia?
No. Mina's team also tested children before and after their first MMR shot. Their antibody libraries stayed intact.
lines.say: No. Mina's team also tested children before and after their first M M R shot. Their antibody libraries stayed intact.

lines.text: The vaccine virus is weakened. It trains your immune system to recognize measles without wiping out the antibody library you already have.
Two doses of MMR are about ninety-seven percent effective at stopping measles. One dose, about ninety-three.
lines.say: Two doses of M M R are about ninety-seven percent effective at stopping measles. One dose, about ninety-three.

lines.text: Kids get the first dose at twelve to fifteen months, and the second between four and six years old.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So why are cases rising again?
Because fewer kids are getting the shots. Kindergarten MMR coverage fell from ninety-five percent in 2019 to about ninety-two percent now.
lines.say: Because fewer kids are getting the shots. Kindergarten M M R coverage fell from ninety-five percent in twenty nineteen to about ninety-two percent now.

lines.text: That sounds small, but it leaves almost three hundred thousand kindergartners unprotected each year. And measles needs about ninety-five percent coverage to be kept out.
Exemptions keep hitting new records, and outbreaks flare wherever many kids in one school or town are unvaccinated, then spread outward.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Can you get your immune memory back?
Partly. Every time a survivor meets an old germ again, the immune system relearns it, cell by cell. But that takes months to years.
And until then, old enemies can strike again: another flu, another ear infection, another chest infection, right when defenses are at their weakest.
So Mina's team suggested a shortcut. After measles, doctors could consider booster shots of earlier routine vaccines, like polio and hepatitis, to refill the lost shelves.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Do adults lose memory too?
The big studies were done in children. Adults are less studied, but adults over twenty are more likely to have measles complications, so protection matters at every age.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: So what should I actually do?
Check your vaccine records. If you're not sure you had two MMR doses, ask your doctor about a blood test or an extra dose. And after a measles infection, ask about catching up on routine vaccines.
lines.say: Check your vaccine records. If you're not sure you had two M M R doses, ask your doctor about a blood test or an extra dose. And after a measles infection, ask about catching up on routine vaccines.

lines.text: Measles doesn't just make you sick. It erases your immune memory.

lines.speaker: q
lines.text: Subscribe for more of the science inside your body, and tell us in the comments: did you ever have measles, or do you know your vaccine record?
